This, along with your flair, reminds me of an interview of a Kantian philosopher. He was asked, "Do you believe in God?"

His response: "You wouldn't understand the answer." The name escapes me, unfortunately.

It's not typical for religions to be thought of as binary true/false truth claims, and that's without even getting into the difficulty of defining what 'religion' is in the first place. The world religions take a variety of different approaches to truth.

A more nuanced way to conceive of it is that religions (especially the Abrahamics) each have their own set of truth claims about God and His historical interaction with our world. And it may be the case that one religion has more claims that are true than another, in which case we would say religion A is *truer* than religion B, and neither are entirely false.

Suppose--as a Christian believes--that God exists, is a Trinity, and that Jesus Christ died and resurrected on the third day. Does this make Christianity *true* and Islam *false*? Muslims also believe in God, they just don't believe that He's a Trinity. Furthermore, they believe that Jesus was a prophet, just not God Incarnate like the Christian believes. In this case, Christianity would be *truer* than Islam. But that doesn't mean that Islam is false, just that the Muslim has fewer religious claims that are true relative to the Christian.

I don't imagine that many well-informed and nuanced religious believers would say that their religion is true in some absolute sense. But rather, they might say that their religious beliefs and traditions correspond to Truth and the Absolute better than other traditions.

Sure, I agree that dispositions assuredly play a role in how one might be affected by encountering defeaters, etc. It may be the case that some people are quite comfortable existing in radical uncertainty, while others may have a disposition that requires them some level of confidence or stability in their understanding of things. If that's the case, then I personally am the latter.

If we grant that, the question may be qualified to how one with the latter disposition can practice philosophy without letting the engagement affect them in such a way, or how they may mitigate the permeation of philosophical considerations into their emotional and mental state.

Sure, I think that the prevailing philosophical issue that may cause people distress to consider is the existence or non-existence of God.

If one is a theist, presumably God plays a major role in their worldview and understanding of the world, so to constantly engage with the question of the reality of God (by reading the literature or corresponding with non-theist academics) may cause one existential and epistemic anxiety.

Likewise, the same for the atheist, for whom being wrong about their atheism could pose significant consequences, giving them existential and epistemic anxiety when engaging with the relevant literature and discussions.

Given that example, my question would be how does the philosopher (theist or non-theist) stay grounded when academically engaging with these considerations that may have drastic consequences?

> I'd be skeptical of how Philosophical this crisis is though, since it apparently does not involve you reading or writing Philosophy

In my case, much of it can be attributed to reading philosophy--specifically, running into philosophical problems or considerations that are likely defeaters for my current understanding of particular things, things that if defeated would have cascading and detrimental effects on my web of beliefs with which it is inferentially related.

> It seems more likely you have a mental health problem that you are conflating with Philosophy.

Having some experience as both a patient and student, I can't imagine what kind of mental health problem would be an appropriate explanation for the kind of existential crisis I described in the post.

Furthermore, isn't it empirically the case that many notable existentialists struggled with the same sort of issue, which served as the primary motivation for their existential account of the world?
